marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q001.takeaway: An adult skeleton has 80 axial bones and 126 appendicular bones.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q001.displayText:
An adult skeleton has 80 axial bones and 126 appendicular bones.

In the adult, 80 bones are present in the axial skeleton, and 126 bones in the appendicular skeleton.
emphasis: An adult skeleton has 80 axial bones and 126 appendicular bones

rationales.a: 88/118 does not match the adult axial and appendicular inventory.
rationales.b: 84/122 miscounts bones in both divisions; standard totals are 80 and 126.
rationales.c: 76/130 shifts four bones from axial to appendicular relative to the standard classification.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q002.takeaway: Bone matrix is rich in type I collagen; type II collagen is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, not bone.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q002.displayText:
Bone matrix is rich in type I collagen; type II collagen is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, not bone.

Bone mainly contains type 1 collagen fibres. Bones are made up of mineralized collagenous extracellular matrix around specialized cells.

The extracellular matrix is composed of: organic component—around 30% of the organic matrix of bone is made up of collagen, mainly type 1 collagen; inorganic component—the major inorganic mineral in the bone matrix is calcium phosphate in the form of microcrystalline hydroxyapatite.

The specialized cells are: osteoblasts—responsible for synthesis, deposition, and mineralization of bone matrix; collagen is synthesized in bone by osteoblasts and osteoblasts become osteocytes after embedding in matrix. Osteocytes are the major cell type of mature bone, distributed throughout the matrix, and have lost the ability to divide or secrete new matrix. Osteoclasts are responsible for local removal of bone during bone growth and remodelling.
emphasis: Bone matrix is rich in type I collagen; type II collagen is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, not bone

rationales.a: Osteocytes are the predominant mature bone cells, so this statement is true.
rationales.b: Osteoblasts synthesize osteoid, including collagen, so this statement is true.
rationales.d: Calcium phosphate mineral, mainly hydroxyapatite, is the major inorganic component.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q003.takeaway: The clavicle is a modified long bone with a shaft and ends but no typical medullary cavity.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q003.displayText:
The clavicle is a modified long bone with a shaft and ends but no typical medullary cavity.

The clavicle is a modified long bone, as it has a modified shaft and no medullary cavity.

Typical long bones have an elongated shaft (diaphysis) and two expanded ends (epiphysis); the shaft has a central medullary cavity and a nutrient foramen directed away from the growing end. Examples include humerus, ulna, radius, femur, tibia and fibula.

Miniature long bones contain only one epiphysis, e.g. metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges. Modified long bones have a modified shaft or ends and no medullary cavity, e.g. clavicle.
emphasis: The clavicle is a modified long bone with a shaft and ends but no typical medullary cavity

rationales.a: The humerus is a typical long bone with a medullary cavity.
rationales.b: The fibula is a typical long bone of the leg.
rationales.c: A metacarpal is classified as a long bone, not the distinctive modified long bone asked here.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q004.takeaway: Os trigonum is an accessory ossicle; fabella, patella and pisiform are sesamoid bones.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q004.displayText:
Os trigonum is an accessory ossicle; fabella, patella and pisiform are sesamoid bones.

Os trigonum is an accessory bone, not a sesamoid bone.

Accessory bones, also known as supernumerary bones, are not always present. They may arise due to an ununited epiphysis developed from extra ossification centres and may be mistaken clinically for fractures.

Examples: Os trigonum—uncommon accessory bone behind the talus, also called lateral tubercle of talus. Os vesalianum—uncommon accessory bone proximal to the fifth metatarsal and found within the peroneus brevis tendon, also known as tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.
emphasis: Os trigonum is an accessory ossicle; fabella, patella and pisiform are sesamoid bones

rationales.a: Fabella is embedded in the tendon of lateral gastrocnemius and is a sesamoid.
rationales.c: Patella is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon.
rationales.d: Pisiform is a sesamoid bone in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q005.takeaway: The maxilla is pneumatic because it contains the air-filled maxillary sinus.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q005.displayText:
The maxilla is pneumatic because it contains the air-filled maxillary sinus.

The maxilla is a pneumatic bone.

Pneumatic bones contain air-filled cavities, making them lightweight; they also aid resonance of sound and act as air-conditioning chambers for inspired air. Examples include maxilla, sphenoid and ethmoid.

Short bones include carpal and tarsal bones. Flat bones include sternum, ribs, scapula and bones of the skull vault. Irregular bones include hip bones, vertebrae and bones in the base of the skull.
emphasis: The maxilla is pneumatic because it contains the air-filled maxillary sinus

rationales.a: Carpal bones are small compact bones and are not pneumatic.
rationales.c: The sternum contains marrow but no air-filled sinus.
rationales.d: The hip bone has no paranasal air sinus and is not pneumatic.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q006.takeaway: Fabella is a sesamoid bone, commonly embedded in the lateral gastrocnemius tendon behind the knee.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q006.displayText:
Fabella is a sesamoid bone, commonly embedded in the lateral gastrocnemius tendon behind the knee.

Fabella is a sesamoid bone. The term describes a bone embedded within a tendon or muscle. It is a normal anatomic variant present in 10% to 30% of individuals and is found within the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, where it moves over the lateral femoral condyle.

Important sesamoid bones: patella—the largest sesamoid bone in the quadriceps femoris tendon; pisiform—in flexor carpi ulnaris; fabella—in the lateral head of gastrocnemius; two sesamoids at the first metacarpal within tendons of flexor pollicis brevis and adductor pollicis; two sesamoids at the first metatarsophalangeal articulation within the double tendon of flexor hallucis brevis.
emphasis: Fabella is a sesamoid bone, commonly embedded in the lateral gastrocnemius tendon behind the knee

rationales.a: Fabella is a sesamoid bone rather than merely an accessory ossicle category in this classification.
rationales.b: It contains no air-filled cavity and is not pneumatic.
rationales.d: Its tendon location and morphology identify it as sesamoid, not an irregular bone.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q007.takeaway: Haversian osteons are characteristic of compact bone and are absent from cancellous trabeculae.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q007.displayText:
Haversian osteons are characteristic of compact bone and are absent from cancellous trabeculae.

The Haversian system is seen in compact bone, not cancellous bone.

Compact bones are composed of cylindrical structural units called Haversian systems or osteons. Each contains a central canal with small blood vessels, nerves and endosteum, surrounded by multiple lamellae of calcified matrix containing type I collagen fibres; these canals communicate through Volkmann's canals.

The lamellae of cancellous/spongy bone are arranged in a meshwork and do not form Haversian systems. The diaphysis and outer cortex of long bones are predominantly compact bone, while the epiphysis and inner medulla are predominantly cancellous bone.
emphasis: Haversian osteons are characteristic of compact bone and are absent from cancellous trabeculae

rationales.a: Cancellous bone is abundant in epiphyses beneath a thin compact shell.
rationales.b: Cancellous bone is internal; the outer cortex is compact bone.
rationales.d: Compact bone is arranged in osteons/lamellae, not a meshwork of trabeculae.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q008.takeaway: Periosteum is continuous with the fibrous capsule where it covers a bone near a joint; it is richly innervated.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q008.displayText:
Periosteum is continuous with the fibrous capsule where it covers a bone near a joint; it is richly innervated.

The X-ray shows Codman's triangle, due to an irregular periosteal reaction commonly seen in osteosarcoma. The periosteum is a thick fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of all bones except joint surfaces and tendon/ligament insertion points (entheses). At the articular margin, the periosteum is continuous with the joint capsule.

The periosteum has two layers: outer fibrous layer containing fibroblasts; inner cambium/osteogenic layer containing progenitor cells that develop into osteoblasts. It is nourished by periosteal arteries and has a rich nerve supply, making it the most sensitive part of bone.
emphasis: Periosteum is continuous with the fibrous capsule where it covers a bone near a joint; it is richly innervated

rationales.a: Periosteum has an outer fibrous layer and inner osteogenic layer, not three fibrous layers.
rationales.b: Osteoprogenitor cells are in the inner cambium layer, not the outer fibrous layer.
rationales.d: Periosteum has sensory nerves and is pain-sensitive; it is not devoid of nerve supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q009.takeaway: Sharpey (perforating) fibers anchor periosteum to underlying bone.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q009.displayText:
Sharpey (perforating) fibers anchor periosteum to underlying bone.

Sharpey's fibers are thick collagen fibers that connect the periosteum to the underlying bone.

They are present in bone and teeth: in bone they tether periosteum to underlying bone; in teeth they connect cementum to the periosteum of the alveolar bone (tooth socket).
emphasis: Sharpey (perforating) fibers anchor periosteum to underlying bone

rationales.a: Sharpey fibers do not join periosteum to synovial membrane.
rationales.b: Their classic osseous role is periosteal attachment to bone, not capsule-to-periosteum linkage.
rationales.d: Enamel-to-dentin is not the connection made by Sharpey fibers in bone.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q010.takeaway: The frontal bone develops by intramembranous ossification, directly from mesenchyme.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q010.displayText:
The frontal bone develops by intramembranous ossification, directly from mesenchyme.

Frontal bones undergo intramembranous ossification; the other listed bones undergo enchondral ossification.

Membranous (dermal) bones form through intramembranous ossification, with direct bone formation in highly vascular mesenchymal membranes; examples include frontal, lacrimal, zygomatic and nasal bones. Cartilaginous bones form by intra-cartilaginous/enchondral ossification of a preformed hyaline cartilage model; examples include bones of limbs, vertebral column and thoracic cage. Membranocartilaginous bones ossify from both cartilage and mesenchymal condensation; examples include clavicle, mandible, occipital bone, temporal bone and sphenoid bone.
emphasis: The frontal bone develops by intramembranous ossification, directly from mesenchyme

rationales.a: Ribs form largely by endochondral ossification from cartilaginous models.
rationales.b: Tibia is a long bone formed by endochondral ossification.
rationales.d: Humerus develops endochondrally from a cartilage model.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q011.takeaway: The greater trochanter is a traction apophysis because muscles attach there and exert pull during growth.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q011.displayText:
The greater trochanter is a traction apophysis because muscles attach there and exert pull during growth.

The marked muscle is piriformis and inserts at the greater trochanter of the femur, which is a traction epiphysis.

Traction epiphysis is nonarticular and does not transmit weight. It provides attachment to one or more tendons exerting traction on the epiphysis. Examples include greater and lesser tubercles of humerus and greater and lesser trochanters of femur.
emphasis: The greater trochanter is a traction apophysis because muscles attach there and exert pull during growth

rationales.a: A pressure epiphysis forms an articular, weight-transmitting surface, unlike the greater trochanter.
rationales.c: Atavistic epiphysis represents a bone that was independently present in ancestral forms.
rationales.d: Aberrant epiphysis is an occasional, non-typical secondary center rather than a muscle-pull site.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q012.takeaway: The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage where long-bone lengthening occurs by endochondral ossification.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q012.displayText:
The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage where long-bone lengthening occurs by endochondral ossification.

The structure marked X is the epiphyseal plate. It is the site for enchondral ossification mainly responsible for growth of long bones.

The epiphyseal/growth plate is a hyaline-cartilage layer separating epiphysis from metaphysis. It receives nourishment from both epiphyseal and metaphyseal arteries. Fractures involving epiphyseal plates are Salter-Harris fractures.

Growing ends: upper limb—upper end of humerus and lower ends of radius and ulna; lower limb—lower end of femur and upper end of tibia.
emphasis: The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage where long-bone lengthening occurs by endochondral ossification

rationales.a: The growth plate is hyaline, not elastic, cartilage.
rationales.b: The plate receives metaphyseal and epiphyseal blood supply patterns; it is not supplied only by epiphyseal arteries.
rationales.c: It separates epiphysis from metaphysis during growth, not the entire epiphysis from diaphysis.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q013.takeaway: The fibula violates the rule because its lower secondary center appears first but fuses before the upper center.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q013.displayText:
The fibula violates the rule because its lower secondary center appears first but fuses before the upper center.

The fibula violates the law of ossification stating that the secondary ossification center that appears first is the last to fuse.

The secondary ossification center at the lower end of the fibula appears before the upper-end center and fuses before the upper end.

Primary centers appear before birth, usually during late embryonic or early fetal life (seventh week to fourth month), and form the diaphysis. Secondary centers usually appear after birth and form the epiphysis.
emphasis: The fibula violates the rule because its lower secondary center appears first but fuses before the upper center

rationales.a: The radius follows the usual sequence: its first secondary center is the last to fuse.
rationales.c: The ulna does not provide the classic violation described for the fibula.
rationales.d: The sternum is not a long-bone example for the secondary epiphysis rule.

marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q014.takeaway: The nutrient artery mainly supplies marrow and inner two-thirds of cortex; the outer third receives periosteal vessels.
marrow__ANAT_CH60_Q014.displayText:
The nutrient artery mainly supplies marrow and inner two-thirds of cortex; the outer third receives periosteal vessels.

The nutrient artery does not nourish the outer one-third of the cortex.

The nutrient artery enters the bone shaft through the nutrient foramen and runs obliquely through the cortex. Nutrient arteries of long bones are directed away from the dominant growing epiphysis because the growing bone might pull and rupture the artery. The source mnemonic is: 'To the elbow, I go, from the knee I flee.'
emphasis: The nutrient artery mainly supplies marrow and inner two-thirds of cortex; the outer third receives periosteal vessels

rationales.a: The nutrient artery supplies the marrow and medullary cavity.
rationales.b: The inner two-thirds of the cortex is supplied by the nutrient artery.
rationales.d: Metaphyseal arteries supply the metaphysis, so it is not the unserved region.
